oneLine: A visual binary: the brightest star in the sky, orbited by a white dwarf every 50.13 years.

what.text: Sirius is a visual binary: the metallic-line A1 V star Sirius A is orbited by the white dwarf Sirius B with a period of 50.13 years.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type A0mA1Va and a parallax of 379.21 +/- 1.58 mas for Sirius.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 32349

why.text: Bond et al. call Sirius A the brightest star in the sky and Sirius B the brightest and nearest white dwarf.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

why.text: The orbit gives dynamical masses of 2.063 +/- 0.023 solar masses for Sirius A and 1.018 +/- 0.011 for Sirius B.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

discovery.text: The orbital solution uses nearly 2300 historical measurements dating back to the 19th century, almost 20 years of photographic observations and about two decades of Hubble images.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

interesting.text: The gravitational redshift of Sirius B measured with Hubble (80.65 +/- 0.77 km/s) gives a mass of 1.017 +/- 0.025 solar masses, in agreement with the dynamical mass.

references.label: Joyce et al. 2018, The gravitational redshift of Sirius B (arXiv:1809.01240)

interesting.text: The Hubble astrometry rules out third bodies orbiting either star down to roughly 15-25 Jupiter masses.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

uncertain.text: Bond et al. give the age of Sirius B as about 228 +/- 10 Myr and that of Sirius A as about 237-247 Myr from evolutionary models.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

uncertain.text: Bond et al. say the two stars probably interacted in the past, although there is no direct evidence for this, and that the orbital eccentricity remains high; they list both as open puzzles.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

uncertain.text: To fit Sirius A in the luminosity-radius plane the models had to assume a slightly sub-solar metallicity of about 0.85 solar.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

studiedBy.role: Imaging astrometry of the binary and STIS spectroscopy for the Sirius B gravitational redshift

reference.label: Bond et al. 2017, The Sirius System and its Astrophysical Puzzles (arXiv:1703.10625)

oneLine: A red supergiant; published distance estimates differ, from about 168 pc to about 220 pc.

what.text: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant, described by Montarges et al. as the second-closest red supergiant to Earth.

references.label: Montarges et al. 2021/2022, A dusty veil shading Betelgeuse during its Great Dimming (arXiv:2201.10551)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type M1-M2Ia-Iab and a parallax of 6.55 +/- 0.83 mas.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 27989

why.text: Red supergiants are the final evolutionary stage of stars with initial masses of 8 to 35 solar masses, a stage that lasts roughly 100,000 years.

references.label: Montarges et al. 2021/2022, A dusty veil shading Betelgeuse during its Great Dimming (arXiv:2201.10551)

why.text: Joyce et al. place Betelgeuse in the core helium-burning phase near the base of the red supergiant branch, with a present-day mass of 16.5-19 solar masses.

references.label: Joyce et al. 2020, New mass and distance estimates for Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.09837)

interesting.text: From November 2019 to March 2020 its visual brightness dropped to 1.614 +/- 0.008 magnitudes around 7-13 February 2020, an event called the Great Dimming.

references.label: Montarges et al. 2021/2022, A dusty veil shading Betelgeuse during its Great Dimming (arXiv:2201.10551)

interesting.text: High-resolution imaging showed the southern hemisphere was ten times darker than usual in visible light, and the authors support a scenario of a dust clump formed above a cool patch on the photosphere.

references.label: Montarges et al. 2021/2022, A dusty veil shading Betelgeuse during its Great Dimming (arXiv:2201.10551)

interesting.text: Joyce et al. report a dominant period of about 400 days that they attribute to fundamental-mode pulsation, and detect a first radial overtone at 185 +/- 13.5 days in SMEI photometry.

references.label: Joyce et al. 2020, New mass and distance estimates for Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.09837)

uncertain.text: Joyce et al. derive a distance of 168 (+27, -15) pc from stellar models, and note it agrees with Hipparcos but less well with recent radio measurements.

references.label: Joyce et al. 2020, New mass and distance estimates for Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.09837)

uncertain.text: Montarges et al. quote a distance of roughly 220 pc.

references.label: Montarges et al. 2021/2022, A dusty veil shading Betelgeuse during its Great Dimming (arXiv:2201.10551)

uncertain.text: The SIMBAD parallax has an uncertainty of 0.83 mas on 6.55 mas (about 13%), and the model-based and other published distances (168 and about 220 pc) differ from each other by more than that.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 27989

uncertain.text: Joyce et al. describe their mass as slightly lower than typical literature values; the mass is a model result, not a direct measurement.

references.label: Joyce et al. 2020, New mass and distance estimates for Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.09837)

studiedBy.role: Spatially resolved ultraviolet spectra before and during the Great Dimming

reference.label: Dupree et al. 2020, Spatially resolved ultraviolet spectroscopy of the Great Dimming of Betelgeuse (arXiv:2008.04945)

studiedBy.role: Space-based photometry used to find the pulsation periods

reference.label: Joyce et al. 2020, New mass and distance estimates for Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.09837)

oneLine: The Sun's closest known stellar neighbour, a red dwarf about 1.3 parsecs away.

what.text: Anglada-Escude et al. describe Proxima Centauri as the Sun's closest stellar neighbour, at a distance of 1.295 parsecs.

references.label: Anglada-Escude et al. 2016, A terrestrial planet candidate in a temperate orbit around Proxima Centauri (arXiv:1609.03449)

what.text: Its effective temperature is about 3050 K, its luminosity about 0.1 per cent of the Sun, its measured radius 0.14 solar radii and its mass about 12 per cent of the Sun.

references.label: Anglada-Escude et al. 2016, A terrestrial planet candidate in a temperate orbit around Proxima Centauri (arXiv:1609.03449)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type M5.5Ve and a parallax of 768.0665 +/- 0.0499 mas.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 70890

why.text: Kervella et al. conclude that Proxima and Alpha Centauri AB are gravitationally bound with a high degree of confidence, with an orbital period of about 550,000 years.

references.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

why.text: The NASA Exoplanet Archive composite table lists two planets for Proxima Centauri: Proxima Cen b (discovered 2016) and Proxima Cen d (discovered 2025).

references.label: NASA Exoplanet Archive, Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table, host Proxima Cen

discovery.text: The bound status comes from an orbit fit with eccentricity 0.50 (+0.08, -0.09); Kervella et al. express it as high confidence, not certainty.

references.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

discovery.text: The orbital phase is currently close to apastron (13.0 kau) and the periastron distance is 4.3 (+1.1, -0.9) kau.

references.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

interesting.text: Proxima and Alpha Centauri AB have almost identical distances and proper motions with respect to the Sun.

references.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

uncertain.text: Kervella et al. state that whether Proxima forms a bound triple system with Alpha Centauri had been an open question since Proxima was discovered a century earlier.

references.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

uncertain.text: Proxima is considered a moderately active star, with a rotation period of about 83 days.

references.label: Anglada-Escude et al. 2016, A terrestrial planet candidate in a temperate orbit around Proxima Centauri (arXiv:1609.03449)

studiedBy.role: High-precision absolute radial velocities of Proxima used to test the bound orbit

reference.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

oneLine: A G2 V star in a close binary with Alpha Centauri B; mass about 1.13 solar masses.

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type G2V for Alpha Centauri A, with a parallax of 742.12 +/- 1.4 mas.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 71683

what.text: Pourbaix & Boffin derive a mass of 1.13 solar masses for component A from a full three-dimensional orbit of the pair.

references.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

why.text: Pourbaix & Boffin note that the alpha Cen system is used for calibration purposes in several studies.

references.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

why.text: Kervella et al. show that the pair is bound to Proxima Centauri with a high degree of confidence.

references.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

uncertain.text: Pourbaix & Boffin say the parallax of alpha Cen is still far from being carved in stone, and any derivation of the individual masses is therefore uncertain.

references.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

uncertain.text: Their masses (1.13 and 0.97 solar) are described as in excellent agreement with the latest asteroseismologic results.

references.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

studiedBy.role: Ten years of radial velocities used to complete the visual orbit into a 3D orbit

reference.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

oneLine: A K1 V star in a close binary with Alpha Centauri A; mass about 0.97 solar masses.

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type K1V for Alpha Centauri B, with a parallax of 742.12 +/- 1.4 mas (the same value as component A).

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 71681

what.text: Pourbaix & Boffin derive a mass of 0.97 solar masses for component B from a full three-dimensional orbit of the pair.

references.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

why.text: Pourbaix & Boffin note that the alpha Cen system is used for calibration purposes in several studies.

references.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

why.text: Kervella et al. show that the pair is bound to Proxima Centauri with a high degree of confidence.

references.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495)

uncertain.text: Pourbaix & Boffin say the parallax of alpha Cen is still far from being carved in stone, and any derivation of the individual masses is therefore uncertain.

references.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

uncertain.text: SIMBAD lists an identical parallax for components A and B, so it should be read as a value for the pair rather than two independent measurements.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 71681
SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 71683

studiedBy.role: Ten years of radial velocities used to complete the visual orbit into a 3D orbit

reference.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636)

oneLine: A red dwarf 1.8 pc away with the largest apparent motion of any known stellar object.

what.text: Ribas et al. describe Barnard's star (Gl 699) as a red dwarf at 1.8 parsecs with the largest apparent motion of any known stellar object.

references.label: Ribas et al. 2018, A candidate super-Earth planet orbiting near the snow line of Barnard's star (arXiv:1811.05955)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type M4V, a parallax of 546.9759 +/- 0.0401 mas and a proper motion of about 10362 mas/yr in declination.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 87937

what.text: It is among the least magnetically active red dwarfs known and has an estimated age older than the Solar System.

references.label: Ribas et al. 2018, A candidate super-Earth planet orbiting near the snow line of Barnard's star (arXiv:1811.05955)

why.text: It is the closest single star to the Sun, second only to the alpha Centauri system.

references.label: Ribas et al. 2018, A candidate super-Earth planet orbiting near the snow line of Barnard's star (arXiv:1811.05955)

discovery.text: Gonzalez Hernandez et al. (2024) confirmed a sub-Earth-mass planet with a 3.15-day period and minimum mass 0.37 +/- 0.05 Earth masses using 156 ESPRESSO observations over four years.

references.label: Gonzalez Hernandez et al. 2024, A sub-Earth-mass planet orbiting Barnard's star (arXiv:2410.00569)

discovery.text: Basant et al. (2025) used 112 MAROON-X radial velocities to confirm planet b and report four planets with minimum masses of 0.19 to 0.34 Earth masses.

references.label: Basant et al. 2025, Four sub-Earth planets orbiting Barnard's Star from MAROON-X and ESPRESSO (arXiv:2503.08095)

discovery.text: The NASA Exoplanet Archive composite table lists Barnard b (2024) and Barnard c, d and e (2025) with periods 3.154, 4.124, 2.340 and 6.739 days.

references.label: NASA Exoplanet Archive, Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table, host Barnard's star

uncertain.text: A 2018 candidate planet at 233 days (minimum mass 3.2 Earth masses) was not supported by later ESPRESSO data, which found no evidence for it.

references.label: Ribas et al. 2018, A candidate super-Earth planet orbiting near the snow line of Barnard's star (arXiv:1811.05955)
Gonzalez Hernandez et al. 2024, A sub-Earth-mass planet orbiting Barnard's star (arXiv:2410.00569)

uncertain.text: Basant et al. state that none of the long history of claimed planet detections around this star had withstood scrutiny before the recent sub-Earth-mass candidates.

references.label: Basant et al. 2025, Four sub-Earth planets orbiting Barnard's Star from MAROON-X and ESPRESSO (arXiv:2503.08095)

uncertain.text: Of the four sub-Earth planets reported in 2025, planets b and e are called confirmed and c and d are still described as candidates in the MAROON-X analysis; their status may change with more data.

references.label: Basant et al. 2025, Four sub-Earth planets orbiting Barnard's Star from MAROON-X and ESPRESSO (arXiv:2503.08095)

studiedBy.role: Radial velocities that revealed the short-period sub-Earth planets

reference.label: Gonzalez Hernandez et al. 2024, A sub-Earth-mass planet orbiting Barnard's star (arXiv:2410.00569)

studiedBy.role: Independent radial velocities used to confirm the planets

reference.label: Basant et al. 2025, Four sub-Earth planets orbiting Barnard's Star from MAROON-X and ESPRESSO (arXiv:2503.08095)

oneLine: A bright A0 V standard star that spins at over 90% of break-up speed and is seen nearly pole-on.

what.text: Vega is the second brightest star in the northern hemisphere and serves as a primary spectral type standard.

references.label: Peterson et al. 2006, Vega is a rapidly rotating star (arXiv:astro-ph/0603520)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type A0V and a parallax of 130.23 +/- 0.36 mas.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 91262

why.text: Vega also serves as the primary photometric calibrator for the ultraviolet and near-infrared through atmosphere models.

references.label: Peterson et al. 2006, Vega is a rapidly rotating star (arXiv:astro-ph/0603520)

why.text: Interferometry shows it is rotating at about 93% of break-up speed (Peterson et al.) or about 91% (Aufdenberg et al.), viewed nearly along its rotation axis.

references.label: Peterson et al. 2006, Vega is a rapidly rotating star (arXiv:astro-ph/0603520)
Aufdenberg et al. 2006, First Results from the CHARA Array VII: Vega (arXiv:astro-ph/0603327)

interesting.text: Peterson et al. note that the star looks too bright compared to its peers and has unusually shaped line profiles, which a pole-on rapid rotator explains.

references.label: Peterson et al. 2006, Vega is a rapidly rotating star (arXiv:astro-ph/0603520)

uncertain.text: The two interferometric studies give different rotation rates (93% and 91% of break-up), so the figure is model dependent.

references.label: Peterson et al. 2006, Vega is a rapidly rotating star (arXiv:astro-ph/0603520)
Aufdenberg et al. 2006, First Results from the CHARA Array VII: Vega (arXiv:astro-ph/0603327)

uncertain.text: Aufdenberg et al. infer an inclination of about 5 degrees and an equatorial velocity of about 275 km/s from a gravity-darkened model.

references.label: Aufdenberg et al. 2006, First Results from the CHARA Array VII: Vega (arXiv:astro-ph/0603327)

uncertain.text: Deep adaptive-optics imaging found no planets or planet candidates; the paper reports only upper limits on any companions.

references.label: Heinze et al. 2008, Deep L and M-band Imaging for Planets Around Vega and epsilon Eridani (arXiv:0807.3975)

studiedBy.role: Long-baseline K-band interferometry of the stellar disc

reference.label: Aufdenberg et al. 2006, First Results from the CHARA Array VII: Vega (arXiv:astro-ph/0603327)

studiedBy.role: Deep L and M band imaging search for planetary-mass companions

reference.label: Heinze et al. 2008, Deep L and M-band Imaging for Planets Around Vega and epsilon Eridani (arXiv:0807.3975)

oneLine: The nearest and brightest classical Cepheid; its distance is contested between Hipparcos and Hubble.

what.text: Polaris is the nearest and brightest classical Cepheid, in a single-lined spectroscopic binary with an orbital period of about 30 years.

references.label: Evans et al. 2008, Direct Detection of the Close Companion of Polaris with the Hubble Space Telescope (arXiv:0806.4904)

what.text: SIMBAD gives type classical Cepheid, spectral type F8Ib and a Hipparcos parallax of 7.54 +/- 0.11 mas.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 11767

why.text: Bond et al. call Polaris a potential anchor point for the Leavitt period-luminosity relation, which is why its distance matters.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, Hubble Space Telescope Trigonometric Parallax of Polaris B (arXiv:1712.08139)

why.text: Hubble directly detected the close companion Polaris Ab at a separation of 0.17 arcsec and confirmed orbital motion a year later.

references.label: Evans et al. 2008, Direct Detection of the Close Companion of Polaris with the Hubble Space Telescope (arXiv:0806.4904)

interesting.text: The 2008 mass for Polaris Aa was the first purely dynamical mass determined for any Cepheid.

references.label: Evans et al. 2008, Direct Detection of the Close Companion of Polaris with the Hubble Space Telescope (arXiv:0806.4904)

uncertain.text: Bond et al. measured a Hubble parallax of 6.26 +/- 0.24 mas for Polaris B, smaller than the Hipparcos 7.54 mas, while others advocate about 10 mas; the distance is described as a matter of contention.

references.label: Bond et al. 2017, Hubble Space Telescope Trigonometric Parallax of Polaris B (arXiv:1712.08139)

uncertain.text: The dynamical mass of the Cepheid, 3.45 +/- 0.75 solar masses in the 2018 update, is described by the authors as preliminary.

references.label: Evans et al. 2018, The Orbit of the Close Companion of Polaris (arXiv:1807.06115)

uncertain.text: The 2008 estimate for Polaris Aa was 4.5 (+2.2, -1.4) solar masses, with the companion Ab at 1.26 (+0.14, -0.07); the 2018 orbit update revised the orbital period to 29.59 years.

references.label: Evans et al. 2008, Direct Detection of the Close Companion of Polaris with the Hubble Space Telescope (arXiv:0806.4904)
Evans et al. 2018, The Orbit of the Close Companion of Polaris (arXiv:1807.06115)

studiedBy.mission: Hubble Space Telescope (ACS, WFPC2, WFC3, FGS)
studiedBy.role: Imaging of the close companion and a trigonometric parallax of Polaris B

reference.label: Bond et al. 2017, Hubble Space Telescope Trigonometric Parallax of Polaris B (arXiv:1712.08139)

oneLine: A nearby blue supergiant (B8 Ia) with alpha Cygni-type pulsation variability.

what.text: Moravveji et al. describe Rigel (beta Ori, B8 Ia) as a nearby blue supergiant displaying alpha Cygni type variability.

references.label: Moravveji et al. 2012, Asteroseismology of the Nearby SN-II Progenitor: Rigel Part I (arXiv:1201.0843)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type B8Ia and a parallax of 3.78 +/- 0.34 mas.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 24436

why.text: The authors call it one of the nearest type-II supernova progenitors, and an excellent test bed for the internal structure of pre core-collapse stars.

references.label: Moravveji et al. 2012, Asteroseismology of the Nearby SN-II Progenitor: Rigel Part I (arXiv:1201.0843)

interesting.text: 28 days of MOST photometry and over 6 years of spectroscopy revealed nineteen significant pulsation modes with time scales from 1.21 to 74.7 days.

references.label: Moravveji et al. 2012, Asteroseismology of the Nearby SN-II Progenitor: Rigel Part I (arXiv:1201.0843)

uncertain.text: The parallax uncertainty is 0.34 mas on 3.78 mas, so the distance is uncertain by roughly one tenth.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 24436

uncertain.text: That Rigel will end as a core-collapse supernova is an expectation from stellar evolution theory, not an observation.

references.label: Moravveji et al. 2012, Asteroseismology of the Nearby SN-II Progenitor: Rigel Part I (arXiv:1201.0843)

studiedBy.role: Space photometry for the pulsation analysis

reference.label: Moravveji et al. 2012, Asteroseismology of the Nearby SN-II Progenitor: Rigel Part I (arXiv:1201.0843)

oneLine: A red giant of about 25 solar radii and 1.08 solar masses (Ramirez & Allende Prieto 2011).

what.text: Arcturus is a red giant with effective temperature 4286 +/- 30 K, log g 1.66 +/- 0.05 and [Fe/H] of -0.52 +/- 0.04.

references.label: Ramirez & Allende Prieto 2011, Fundamental Parameters and Chemical Composition of Arcturus (arXiv:1109.4425)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type K1.5IIIFe-0.5, a parallax of 88.83 +/- 0.54 mas and proper motion components of -1093.39 and -2000.06 mas/yr.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 69673

why.text: Ramirez & Allende Prieto derive a mass of 1.08 +/- 0.06 solar masses, a radius of 25.4 +/- 0.2 solar radii and an age of 7.1 (+1.5, -1.2) Gyr.

references.label: Ramirez & Allende Prieto 2011, Fundamental Parameters and Chemical Composition of Arcturus (arXiv:1109.4425)

uncertain.text: The surface gravity, mass and age depend on stellar evolution models combined with the parallax, so they are model results rather than direct measurements.

references.label: Ramirez & Allende Prieto 2011, Fundamental Parameters and Chemical Composition of Arcturus (arXiv:1109.4425)

uncertain.text: The effective temperature was determined by fitting model atmospheres to the spectral energy distribution from 0.44 to 10 micrometres.

references.label: Ramirez & Allende Prieto 2011, Fundamental Parameters and Chemical Composition of Arcturus (arXiv:1109.4425)

studiedBy.mission: Ground-based spectroscopy and photometry (spectral energy distribution)
studiedBy.role: Atmospheric parameters and abundances of 17 elements

reference.label: Ramirez & Allende Prieto 2011, Fundamental Parameters and Chemical Composition of Arcturus (arXiv:1109.4425)

oneLine: A red supergiant whose atmosphere has been resolved by ALMA, the VLA and the VLTI.

what.text: Antares is an early-M red supergiant.

references.label: O'Gorman et al. 2020, ALMA and VLA reveal the lukewarm chromospheres of the nearby red supergiants Antares and Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.08023)

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type M1.5Iab+B2Vn (the string includes a B2Vn component) and a parallax of 5.89 +/- 1.0 mas.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 80763

why.text: ALMA and VLA observations resolved free-free emission of the atmosphere at 11 wavelengths; the projected diameter grows from 50.7 mas at 0.7 mm to 431 mas at 10 cm, 1.35 to 11.6 times the photospheric angular diameter.

references.label: O'Gorman et al. 2020, ALMA and VLA reveal the lukewarm chromospheres of the nearby red supergiants Antares and Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.08023)

why.text: VLTI/AMBER images in CO lines show an outer molecular atmosphere (MOLsphere) extending to 1.2-1.4 stellar radii with a temperature of about 2000 K.

references.label: Ohnaka et al. 2013, High spectral resolution imaging of the dynamical atmosphere of Antares (arXiv:1304.4800)

interesting.text: All four ALMA measurements show the atmosphere is elongated, with a flattening of 15% at a similar position angle.

references.label: O'Gorman et al. 2020, ALMA and VLA reveal the lukewarm chromospheres of the nearby red supergiants Antares and Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.08023)

uncertain.text: The parallax uncertainty is 1.0 mas on 5.89 mas, so the distance is uncertain by roughly one sixth.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 80763

uncertain.text: The convective cell sizes (5% to 45% of the angular diameter) come from model fits to VLTI/PIONIER interferometry, and the apparent diameter depends on the position angle sampled.

references.label: Montarges et al. 2017, The convective surface of the red supergiant Antares (arXiv:1705.07829)

uncertain.text: The CO-line appearance of the atmosphere changed drastically within one year, implying a significant change in the velocity field.

references.label: Ohnaka et al. 2013, High spectral resolution imaging of the dynamical atmosphere of Antares (arXiv:1304.4800)

studiedBy.role: Resolved radio continuum emission of the extended atmosphere

reference.label: O'Gorman et al. 2020, ALMA and VLA reveal the lukewarm chromospheres of the nearby red supergiants Antares and Betelgeuse (arXiv:2006.08023)

studiedBy.role: Near-infrared interferometric imaging of the surface and atmosphere

reference.label: Montarges et al. 2017, The convective surface of the red supergiant Antares (arXiv:1705.07829)

oneLine: A nearby Sun-like (G8 V) star with radial-velocity planet signals whose number differs by source.

what.text: SIMBAD gives spectral type G8V and a parallax of 273.8097 +/- 0.1701 mas for tau Ceti.

references.label: SIMBAD (CDS), SIMBAD basic data for HIP 8102

what.text: Dietrich & Apai describe it as the closest single Sun-like star to the Solar System.

references.label: Dietrich & Apai 2020, An Integrated Analysis with Predictions on the Architecture of the tau Ceti Planetary System (arXiv:2010.14675)

why.text: Feng et al. find periodic radial-velocity signals at 20.0, 49.3, 160 and 642 days which they interpret as planets, all with minimum masses below 4 Earth masses.

references.label: Feng et al. 2017, Color difference makes a difference: four planet candidates around tau Ceti (arXiv:1708.02051)

uncertain.text: Feng et al. call these four planet candidates, while Dietrich & Apai write of four confirmed planets, and the NASA Exoplanet Archive composite table lists three (tau Cet f, g, h, with minimum masses from radial velocity).

references.label: Feng et al. 2017, Color difference makes a difference: four planet candidates around tau Ceti (arXiv:1708.02051)
